claims.text: The overall tribo-corrosion degradation of high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic balance between mechanical removal of a protective oxide film and alloy repassivation.
The balance between oxide removal and repassivation controls both the wear and corrosion components of degradation.
The proposed FeCoNiMnCu or similar alloy has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
FeCoNiMnCu-based material can form protective oxide films during oxidative exposure.
Controlled thermal oxidation can pre-form a Cr2O3 layer and a high-entropy spinel oxide on FeCoNiMnCu deposited on SS-304.
Chemical oxidation can pre-form the proposed protective oxide layer.
The relevant surface mediator is a mechanically robust high-entropy spinel or Cr2O3-containing oxide film.
Sliding wear mechanically disrupts the protective oxide film.
Disruption of the oxide film exposes reactive metal.
The exposed metal repassivates by reforming the oxide film.
When repassivation is faster than wear-induced film removal, the intact film limits corrosion.
When wear-induced film removal is faster than repassivation, corrosion and total degradation accelerate.
A pre-oxidized condition with a robust protective film will have lower total degradation than an otherwise matched as-prepared condition.
Pre-oxidation will reduce the corrosion component through more effective repassivation.
The pre-formed oxide film will modify wear behavior.
At high mechanical loads, wear removal can dominate and negate the protective effect of the oxide film.
Highly aggressive electrolytes can prevent formation or stability of the protective oxide film and cause the prediction to fail.
The protective effect should hold when wear rates are moderate and repassivation kinetics are competitive with film removal.
